title: Why Jails Painted Their Cells Bubblegum Pink #shorts

lines.text: Could one color calm down an angry prisoner?
He stared at a bubblegum pink card,
So a Navy jail let him test it.
They painted a whole cell pink, floor to ceiling.
and in fifteen minutes, they calmed right down!
Soon jails everywhere were painting cells pink.
A football coach even painted the other team's locker room pink!
When scientists tested it again, the calm wore off fast,
and a plain gray cell worked just as well.
So can a color calm you down? Maybe, for about fifteen minutes.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Baker-Miller pink': Alexander Schauss tested color responses; staring at a card of the pink reportedly lowered heart rate, pulse and respiration; in 1979 a Navy correctional facility in Seattle painted confinement cells pink (named after directors Baker and Miller); the Navy reported no hostile incidents after March 1, 1979 and that 15 minutes of exposure reduced aggression
Wikipedia, 'Baker-Miller pink': University of Iowa coach Hayden Fry had the visiting team's locker room at Kinnick Stadium painted pink (1979)

Wikipedia, 'Baker-Miller pink': Santa Clara County jail saw inmates calm after 15 minutes but a reverse effect after 20 minutes; Gilliam and Unruh (1988) contradicted the heart-rate claims; Genschow et al. (2014, 59 prisoners) found aggression fell in both pink and gray cells with no difference by color
Mental Floss, 'Soothe Yourself With Drunk Tank Pink' (15 minutes of exposure; Iowa locker room)
